Technical briefing

CQL: what the mathematics can compute, and what it cannot.

Conexus’s core is a language, CQL, in which database schemas are equational theories, data migrations are adjoint functors, and a theorem prover refuses programs that would break stated constraints. This briefing is a capability review: the guarantees, the limits, the scale, and the place of that system among Pregel, classical data exchange, and closer Google work. It is not a review of the firm as a vendor.

Research Lab briefing · Public papers, patents, the open CQL tool and technical documentation · 12 November 2026

On “Pegel from Google” The comparison below treats that name as Pregel, Google’s 2010 large-scale graph-processing system (Malewicz et al., SIGMOD). Confidence in the name is high: no Google project called Pegel was found, and Pregel is a one-letter omission from a well-known paper, named after the river in Königsberg. Confidence that the two systems are peers is low. They occupy different problem classes. The technically interesting question is where a chase-based left Kan extension and a BSP superstep are the same kind of computation — and where they are not. Closer technical analogues (F1 schema change, the Knowledge Graph, Dataflow / Data Fusion, and the academic line of Clio, data exchange and Datalog chase engines) are taken up in the same section.

The technical verdict

A real, implementable alternative to informal ETL — with guarantees that are precise, and narrower than the word “proof” suggests.

  1. The computational core is solid and published. In CQL a schema is a multi-sorted equational theory (intuitively, a directed graph with path equations, plus a type side for attributes). An instance is an algebra of that theory — equivalently, a set-valued functor. A schema mapping is a theory morphism, and it induces three adjoint data-migration functors: Δ (composition, a projection), Σ (its left adjoint: a left Kan extension, computed by a chase), and Π (the right adjoint of Δ: a join-like right Kan extension). Integration of several sources is a colimit given the overlaps the user declares. That package is in the Journal of Functional Programming (Schultz & Wisnesky, 2017), Theory and Applications of Categories (2017), and the Journal of Automated Reasoning (Meyers, Spivak & Wisnesky, 2022), and is implemented in a downloadable Java IDE.
  2. “Provably correct” is a statement about a program and a theory, not about the world. The theorem prover can reject, at compile time, a query or mapping that would materialise an instance violating the stated equations. The result of a successful Σ is universal: unique up to unique isomorphism given those inputs. If the mappings or the identifications are wrong, the “proof” is a correct account of a wrong model. The word problem in finitely presented categories is undecidable in general (the JFP paper is candid about this); the tool relies on practical provers. The chase is complete for finite free models of cartesian theories under fairness assumptions (JAR 2022); it need not terminate on arbitrary theories, and the result may be infinite.
  3. Entity resolution is an input, not an output. Σ along a collapsing functor, with no extra equations, is a disjoint union. To merge two Alices you must declare that they are the same; the universal construction then merges them canonically. Category theory does not discover the match.
  4. Published scale is single-node and in-memory. The community site says so directly. JAR 2022 reports roughly a 10× speed-up over the authors’ own Java ports of earlier left-Kan algorithms, on a MacBook Air, and says the algorithm is “fast enough to support multi-gigabyte real-world use cases.” A 2021 technical demo mentions Spark/Hadoop code generation and, in the same text, that entire enterprise databases “won’t fit” in CQL. There is no public cluster-scale benchmark. That is a different league from Pregel, and a different job.
  5. The closest peers are Clio, data-exchange chase engines and OBDA, not Pregel. The distinctive combination is the adjoint triple, a language with a compile-time prover, and a universal warehouse. A chase-based Σ is a form of iterative fixpoint and can be scheduled in BSP-like rounds — JAR already uses bulk, table-at-a-time steps — but it is iterating a term model, not a vertex program. An LLM-written English query can be checked as a CQL program; that is a real proof of the program, not of the English.

The data model

Start with a small human-resources schema, because every later construction is an operation on objects of this kind. A CQL schema is an algebraic theory: a collection of sorts (entities and types), operations (foreign keys and attributes), and equations between them. The intended meaning of a schema is a category; the intended meaning of an instance is the initial algebra of that theory — a functor from the schema to sets that sends equations to actual equalities.

In the picture below, Emp and Dept are entities. The arrow works is a foreign key, which is required to be a total function: every employee has exactly one department. The attributes ename and dname land in a type, String, which lives on the “type side” of the theory and may carry its own operations (concatenation, and so on). An optional equation — drawn here as a secretary path — is a data-integrity constraint: the secretary of a department works in that department. Any instance, and any migration, must respect it.

Interactive · A schema as a theory, and an instance as a functor

Two remarks that matter later. First, foreign keys in CQL are more rigid than in a typical SQL schema that merely declares a key and hopes the data complies: here they are operations of a theory, and an instance that broke them would not be a model. Second, attributes are not just uninterpreted strings. Because they live in an algebraic theory, the theorem prover can reason about user-defined functions and how they interact with constraints — the central concern of the 2017 TAC paper on algebraic databases.

A schema mapping is a morphism of theories: a translation of sorts and operations that preserves provable equality. In pictures, it is a graph homomorphism that sends declared path-equals to path-equals. If it does not, the prover rejects it at compile time. That is the first sense in which CQL programs are “checked before they run.”

Sources: Spivak, “Functorial Data Migration,” Information and Computation 2012; Schultz, Spivak, Vasilakopoulou & Wisnesky, “Algebraic Databases,” TAC 32 (2017); Schultz & Wisnesky, “Algebraic Data Integration,” JFP 27 (2017). The secretary-style path equation is the standard “the secretary works in the department” constraint used throughout that literature.

The three migrations: Δ, Σ and Π

A schema mapping F : S → T does not, by itself, move data. It induces three canonical ways of moving data, and they are adjoints of one another. That adjunction is the reason later constructions can be called universal rather than merely convenient.

  • ΔF goes backwards, T-instances to S-instances. It is composition: ΔF(I) = I ∘ F. Intuitively a projection, or a lossless decomposition, along F. It is the easy one: no new rows are invented.
  • ΣF is the left adjoint of ΔF, going forwards. It is a left Kan extension of the instance along F, and in CQL it is computed by a chase. Intuitively: an outer union, then a merge of whatever the equations force. It may create labelled nulls (fresh identifiers) for structure that the target requires and the source does not supply. It is the “free” or “least committed” push-forward.
  • ΠF is the right adjoint of ΔF, also going forwards. It is a right Kan extension. Intuitively a join, or a product along F. It is the “most conservative” push-forward: it keeps only what can be seen as a tuple of source data.

The adjunctions, in the form used in the papers, are:

T-Inst( ΣF(I), J ) ≅ S-Inst( I, ΔF(J) )
S-Inst( ΔF(J), I ) ≅ T-Inst( J, ΠF(I) )

In ordinary language: a map out of a Σ-migrated instance is the same thing as a map out of the original instance into a Δ-migrated instance; and dually for Π. That is what “universal” is doing here. It is not a metaphor.

The explainer below takes a mapping that collapses two source entities, Student and Employee, onto one target entity, Person. The input data has two Alices, one on each side. Watch what each functor does — and notice that Σ, on its own, does not decide they are the same person.

Interactive · The same mapping, three results

A query in CQL is a sequence of these functors, written in a for/where/return syntax (JFP 2017). When several source schemas are to be integrated, the design pattern is not “map each source directly onto a warehouse schema.” It is: declare the overlaps (as a span of mappings), take the colimit — the unique-up-to-unique-isomorphism integrated schema and instance compatible with those overlaps — and only then query from that universal warehouse onto the schema you actually wanted. The 2021 warehouse walk-through is this pattern in an investment-management example, including a compile-time check that the final query does not break the target’s constraints, and a provenance record on every output row.

The marketing phrase “eleven sources, eleven mappings, not 110” is a statement about this specification pattern: n mappings into a colimit, rather than n(n−1) pairwise maps. Ordinary hub-and-spoke warehouses also write n maps to a canonical model. The mathematical difference is universality — the integrated schema is determined by the overlaps, and a third mapping can be obtained by composition (the 2026 building-lifecycle preprint demonstrates this for IFC, BRICK and RealEstateCore). Runtime complexity of the chase is a separate question, taken up below.

Sources: JFP 2017, especially the description of Δ as projection, Π as join and Σ as union/chase, and Figure 2; JAR 2022, on Σ as a left Kan extension computed by the chase; the 2021 warehouse demo; Nagy et al., “A Categorical Approach to Semantic Interoperability Across Building Lifecycle,” arXiv:2601.16663, on O(n) specification and composition of mappings.

What a proof is, and how the chase computes Σ

Compile-time checking

CQL’s theorem prover has one essential job: decide, without looking at data, whether a mapping or a query preserves the equations of the theories involved. If a target constraint does not follow from the source constraints and the query definition, the program is rejected. The community site puts this as: a CQL program cannot materialise an instance that violates a data-integrity constraint.

That is a real, useful guarantee, and it is also easy to over-read. The prover is only as good as the equations it is given, and only as decisive as the fragment of equational logic it can settle.

Interactive · What is being proved

The chase, as a left Kan algorithm

Computing Σ — a left Kan extension of a set-valued functor along a schema mapping — is the expensive direction. JAR 2022 shows that it reduces to constructing a free model of a cartesian (finite-limit) theory, and that the standard and parallel chase from database theory compute such models. Under fairness assumptions those chases are complete for finite free models of cartesian theories. The paper’s CQL implementation is a specialised parallel chase, and is the subject of US patent 11,256,672.

Operationally, a round of that algorithm is a bounded sequence of three actions, then a repeat until nothing changes:

  1. Add elements. For each target operation that requires something not yet present, introduce a fresh labelled null (a Skolem identifier).
  2. Add coincidences. For each equation of the target theory, and each equation coming from the mapping, record that two terms denote the same element.
  3. Merge. Identify equal elements, typically in a union-find structure.

That loop is a fixpoint iteration. It is kin, computationally, to a Datalog evaluation and to a Pregel superstep schedule: synchronized rounds, a growing or merging state, a test for quiescence. It is not kin in what the state means. The chase state is a term model of a theory; a Pregel state is a value at each vertex of a graph. Click through a short run below, on the two-Alices example.

Interactive · One chase, two endings

Guarantees, and where they stop

  • Soundness, relative to inputs. If the prover accepts a program, and the chase finishes, the output is a model of the target theory and is universal among such models given the mapping and the source instance. This is the content of the adjunction and of the free-model construction.
  • Decidability. The word problem for finitely presented categories is not decidable in general (JFP 2017, recalling a long-known fact). CQL uses practical techniques — congruence closure, Knuth-Bendix completion in earlier algorithms, and the specialised chase. A query can therefore fail to be decided, not only fail to be correct. That is a capability limit, not a bug in a particular file.
  • Termination. A left Kan extension need not be finite. The chase on a general regular (existential Horn) theory need not terminate. JAR 2022’s completeness result is for cartesian theories — roughly, unique existence (∃!) rather than bare existence — under fairness. Restricting to that fragment is a design choice with a payoff (completeness) and a cost (some data-exchange specifications are not cartesian).
  • Constants versus nulls. The JAR paper discusses the mismatch between category theory’s preference for an unfailing, nulls-only semantics and practical chase engines that refuse to equate two distinct constants. In a data-exchange setting with constants, a chase can fail (a contradiction). That is also a capability: contradiction-detection is useful, and it is not the same as a successful universal model.
  • Nothing here discovers facts about the world. Identifications, overlaps and equations are inputs. The universal property then does the most — and only — thing it can with them.

Sources: JFP 2017, §1.2 and the implementation section, on word problems; JAR 2022, §§1, 4–5 and the completeness claims for the standard and parallel chase, the three-action loop, fairness, cartesian theories, and the constant/null discussion; US 11,256,672; categoricaldata.net on compile-time rejection of constraint-violating programs.

Scale, complexity and the published benchmarks

Three different “complexity” claims are easy to conflate, and they should be kept apart.

Specification complexity. Given declared overlaps, n sources can be related by n mappings into a colimit, and further mappings can be obtained by composition (Nagy et al. 2026 state O(n) specification complexity for n building ontologies). This is about how many mappings a person writes, not about how long the chase runs.

Decision complexity. Checking that a mapping preserves equations is a word-problem instance, undecidable in general, practical in the fragments the IDE actually discharges. Evaluating a query in the discrete-algebraic fragment corresponds, the JFP paper shows, to unions of conjunctive queries under bag semantics, and can be delegated to an existing RDBMS. That is the honest reading of “CQL compiles to SQL.”

Chase complexity. Computing Σ is a chase. In general a chase may be exponential in the interesting parameters, may not terminate, and may produce an infinite result. JAR 2022’s implementation stores cardinalities and lists rather than sets, maintains a path-compressed union-find, and runs table-at-a-time (bulk) rounds rather than picking one row non-deterministically. On a 2018 MacBook Air (1.6 GHz i5, 16 GB, Oracle Java 11), on random instances of a “quotient of a set” example, with row counts up to 12 million:

  • The specialised parallel chase is about ten times faster than the authors’ own Java ports of earlier left-Kan algorithms (Bush, Leeming & Walters 2003; a “substitute and saturate” algorithm with Knuth-Bendix or congruence closure). The paper notes they knew of no prior public left-Kan benchmarks, and that random instances “may not be representative of performance in practice.”
  • Time throughput (rows per second) worsens as the input grows, attributed to union-find’s n log n behaviour. Memory throughput (rows per megabyte) improves, attributed to logarithmic space in the same structure.
  • The authors say the algorithm is “fast enough to support multi-gigabyte real-world use cases,” citing their 2019 Computational Materials Science paper (Open Quantum Materials Database integration). That is the largest published performance claim. It is not a cluster figure, and it is not a comparison with Informatica, Spark, a production chase engine, or Pregel.

The open tool’s own scope statement is the right summary: “production-ready for single-node in-memory data processing workloads, such as integrating data for data science,” with scalability “similar to that of SQL and chase engines.” CQL is not a database management system: “it neither stores nor updates data.” The 2021 demo is consistent with this — land a fragment, do not import an entire enterprise database, “they won’t fit” — and additionally claims code generation to Spark and Hadoop. That codegen path is a real architectural hook toward larger runs. No published measurement of it was found.

Published scale, in each system’s own units

The bars are not a unit conversion. They mark that the published figures are of a different order, on different problems.

Sources: Google research blog and SIGMOD 2010 (Pregel: billions of vertices, trillions of edges, thousands of machines); categoricaldata.net and JAR 2022 (CQL: single-node in-memory; multi-gigabyte use cases on a laptop-class benchmark).

Comparisons: Pregel, Google’s closer work, and academic peers

Pregel is a framework for iterative graph algorithms at web scale. Programs are a sequence of supersteps in Valiant’s Bulk Synchronous Parallel model: in each superstep every vertex, conceptually in parallel, reads messages sent in the previous step, updates its state, and sends messages for the next. The 2010 SIGMOD paper reports that PageRank is about 15 lines, and that the system had been used internally on billions of vertices and trillions of edges. It is an internal Google system; the open descendants are Apache Giraph and, in spirit, Spark GraphX.

CQL does not compute PageRank, does not “think like a vertex,” and does not, on the public evidence, run on a thousand-machine cluster. Pregel does not accept a schema theory, does not prove that a mapping preserves equations, and does not compute a universal integrated instance. A comparison is useful only once that is stated. The interesting overlap is narrower: both systems iterate a state to a fixpoint in synchronized rounds. A parallel chase can be scheduled as BSP rounds — JAR’s speed-up is already attributed to bulk, table-at-a-time steps, “consistent with [the finding] of the database theory literature, where parallel versions of the chase are deliberately employed because they are faster than sequential versions.” One could, in principle, implement a distributed chase on Giraph or Dataflow. That is a research composition, not a published Conexus product, and it would still be chasing a theory, not running a vertex program.

Axis CQL The other system

The AI products, taken as a technical question

Conexus’s current site wraps CQL in products that accept English questions, ground large language models, and verify legal citations, and it uses the language of mathematical proof for all of them. The question here is not whether those products should be bought. It is what, technically, a CQL-backed “proof” can mean once a language model is in the loop.

A pipeline that is actually supported by the published core looks like this:

  1. A model, or a person, proposes a CQL mapping or query — possibly from an English question.
  2. The theorem prover checks that program against the schemas and equations on hand.
  3. If the program is accepted and the chase (or the compiled SQL) finishes, the result is a model of the target theory, with provenance, and with a proof that this program preserves these constraints.

Step 2 is the genuine formal check. It will catch a query that drops a key, a mapping that breaks a path equation, a warehouse load that cannot satisfy a target constraint. That is already more than ordinary RAG, and it is exactly what CQL was designed to do.

It will not catch a fluent, well-typed translation of the wrong question. “Revenue by region last quarter” and “revenue by region last quarter, excluding returns” can both be perfect CQL. The prover blesses both. The proof is of the program, not of the English. The same gap exists for a mapping an LLM proposes: if it identifies the wrong two Alices, Σ will merge them canonically and the prover will be satisfied.

A tighter design follows from the same observation and is technically honest: the model is allowed to emit only CQL, never a number; the number comes from executing a checked program; any natural-language gloss is labelled as unchecked. That reduces hallucination of values. It does not reduce hallucination of intent, and it does not make “no hallucinations possible” a theorem. That sentence, on the Knowledge Amplification page, does not follow from the published mathematics.

Two other products sit at different distances from the core. Project Integrity and the 2022 spreadsheet preprint (Chevron-affiliated co-authors, a MASP casing-pressure case) are aligned with it: documents and sheets as theories, conflicts as failures of a merge or a chase, a proof that a specification is inconsistent relative to declared structure. That is CQL’s job. Litigation Intelligence — classify a legal citation as verified, flagged, or unverifiable against a corpus — is a retrieval and look-up problem. Nothing in the CQL papers describes that task; a Kan extension is not what tells you a case was overruled. It can be a useful product and still be a different technical artefact, borrowing the word “proof” from the core.

Sources: the guarantees in JFP 2017 and JAR 2022, as bounded in §4 above; Query Intelligence, Knowledge Amplification (“No hallucinations possible”), Litigation Intelligence, Project Integrity; Baylor, Hansen, Montero, Daimler & Wisnesky, “Consensus-Free Spreadsheet Integration,” arXiv:2209.14457.

Experiments worth running

The public CQL IDE — at categoricaldata.net and in GitHub releases — is the right instrument. The README licences it for non-commercial and exploratory commercial use, which covers the work below. These are measurements and attempts at breakage, not questions for a sales call.

1. Reproduce a built-in example, then break it.
The IDE ships demonstrations from the papers (the JFP and algebraic-database examples, the APG program, finance-colimit warehouses). Run one to completion. Then comment out a single where condition, as the 2021 demo does with the portfolio-holding query, and confirm that the prover rejects the program without touching data. That is the compile-time guarantee in actual use.
2. Exhibit a wrong mapping that still proves.
On a two-source merge, write an overlap that identifies the wrong records (the two Alices who are not the same person, or two columns that merely share a name). Confirm that Σ merges them and that the prover is satisfied. This is the cleanest way to feel the relativity of the guarantee: soundness given inputs, not correspondence to the world.
3. Measure Σ against the JAR claims, on hardware you know.
The paper’s headline is a 10× speed-up versus the authors’ ports of earlier left-Kan algorithms, on random instances of one running example, on a 2018 MacBook Air, up to 12 million rows, with time throughput worsening and memory throughput improving as n grows. Rebuild a “quotient of a set” instance at several sizes, record wall-clock and peak RSS, and plot rows against time. You will not be able to repeat their exact baseline algorithms unless those are still in the IDE; you will be able to test whether multi-million-row, multi-gigabyte runs are routine on a single node in 2026, which is the practically relevant part of the claim.
4. Look for non-termination and for prover timeouts.
JAR’s completeness result is for cartesian theories under fairness. Write a small non-cartesian or cyclic specification (an unconstrained existential, or a theory whose left Kan extension is infinite) and record what the IDE does: a timeout, a diagnostic, a hang, a finite approximation. The same for a word-problem that congruence closure should not decide. A capability review needs the failure mode, not only the happy path.
5. Round-trip through SQL.
JFP 2017 and the 2021 demo both describe compiling CQL queries to SQL (as views) and landing data over JDBC. Take a modest real schema you already trust, land a fragment, write a CQL query, export SQL, and compare results and plans with a hand-written query. This tests whether the “delegate to an RDBMS” path is usable, and whether provenance survives the export as the demo claims.
6. Build a four-schema colimit and a composed mapping.
The distinctive design pattern is the universal warehouse, and the 2026 building-lifecycle preprint claims that two explicit mappings can yield a third by composition. Recreate a miniature IFC / BRICK / RealEstateCore-style span, or three of your own schemas, and check that the composed mapping agrees with a hand-written third. Then change one overlap and watch the colimit move. That is the O(n) specification claim, in a size you can inspect.
7. If you want a Pregel-shaped comparison, compare the iteration, not the product.
Time a CQL chase on a graph-like schema (a path-equation quotient, an APG example) against a short Giraph or GraphX job on the same graph that computes a similar fixpoint — connected components, or equality saturation of a relation. Do not expect a meaningful “CQL versus Pregel” performance winner. Do expect a concrete sense of what is in the state at each round, and of when the chase is inventing labelled nulls that no vertex program would invent. That is the composition question in §7, made empirical.
